result.summary: Pausanias continues describing victor statues at Olympia, starting with the Acarnian pancratiast Xenarches and several Spartan horse-breeders, including Lichas, who was scourged for entering under Theban colours. He then describes the statue of the seer Thrasybulus, and the statues of Timosthenes, Antipater, Timon, Æsypus, a Samian boxer and the Messenian boy Damiscus.

scenes.title: Xenarches and Spartan horse-breeders
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the statue of Xenarches and those of the Spartan horse-breeders Lycinus, Arcesilaus and Lichas. He tells how Lichas was scourged for entering as a Theban, which led to the war at the Altis.
scenes.stakes: Lichas risked punishment, and Sparta's exclusion from the games led to conflict with Elis.

scenes.title: Thrasybulus the seer
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the statue of the Elean seer Thrasybulus, with its lizard and split dog, and comments on his divination and the Iamidæ.

scenes.title: Boys, boxers and a tyrant's bribe
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists statues of Timosthenes, Antipater, Timon and Æsypus and the Samian boxer. Antipater refused a bribe from Dionysius' agents and kept his Milesian identity.
scenes.stakes: Antipater could have gained a tyrant's favour but chose to keep his city's honour.

scenes.title: Damiscus and the Messenians
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the Messenian boy Damiscus and notes that Messenian luck at Olympia failed during their exile and returned with their restoration.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias notes the striking link between Messenian exile and their failure at Olympia.

analysis.text: The passage shows how athletic victories carried civic pride and politics, as with Antipater's loyalty to Miletus and Lichas's Theban entry.
Sparta's exclusion from the games and the war with Elis reflect how Olympia was entangled with Greek interstate rivalries.

fun_facts.text: Eutychides' statue of the Fortune of Antioch on the Orontes was widely copied in antiquity; Roman copies survive.

language_notes.text: Pancratiast: a competitor in the pancratium, a brutal combination of wrestling and boxing with very few rules.
The invasion of the Medes means the Persian invasion of Greece (480–479 BC); Greeks often called the Persians Medes.
Colts were entered in a separate race for young horses; when his colt was rejected, he entered it among the full-grown horses instead and won.
Riband means ribbon; tying one on the winning charioteer publicly declared the victory as one's own.
The Umpires are the Hellanodikai, the Elean judges of the Olympic games, who could punish offenders with flogging.
This refers to the Spartan war against Elis around 420–400 BC, in which fighting reached the Altis, the sacred precinct of Olympia.
Thrasybulus served as seer for the Mantineans in a war against Sparta; Pausanias promises fuller details in his Arcadian book.
"Effigy" means statue. The dog is cut in half as a sacrificial victim, its liver displayed for reading omens.
Pindar's Olympian Ode 6 tells how Iamus, son of Apollo, received the gift of prophecy. The Iamidæ were an Elean family of seers.
"The course" means the footrace; "prize for boys" refers to the boys' age-class at the games.
Dionysius is the tyrant of Syracuse. Syracusans sought a victory for their city to bring him prestige.
Zancle was the earlier name of Messana in Sicily. The Strait is the Strait of Messina.

context_notes.text: Lysippus of Sicyon was a leading fourth-century BC bronze sculptor, famed for his many statues of athletes and of Alexander.
Myro (Myron) was a famous Athenian sculptor of the fifth century BC, best known for his Discus-thrower.
Sparta was barred from the games because of a dispute with Elis, so Spartans could not enter openly under their own name.
Under the usual rule the owner of the horses, not the driver, was named victor, so Elis recorded the Thebans as winners.
Eutychides' Fortune (Tyche) of Antioch on the Orontes was a celebrated statue of the city's guardian goddess.
The Altis was the sacred precinct of Zeus at Olympia, where victor statues were set up.
The Messenians were driven from the Peloponnese by Sparta and lived in exile until their restoration, which Pausanias treats elsewhere.

literary_notes.text: The brief sentence reports a public flogging flatly, and its plainness makes the humiliation and the later consequences seem sharper.
Lichas fought a war over his honour and set up a statue, yet the official Elean records deny him the victory.
The lizard and the split dog serve as emblems of Thrasybulus' prophetic craft, identifying him by his method.
Antipater's refusal of the bribe and his inscription show civic pride and integrity.
Pausanias pauses to remark on the coincidence, offering his own interpretation of events.
Luck returning with the homeland's restoration reinforces the link between fortune and exile that runs through his Messenian story.
